title: Anterior and Medial Thigh: Quadriceps Femoris and Obturator Innervation

steps.tx: The anterior compartment of the thigh is dominated by the **quadriceps femoris**, the great extensor muscle of the knee joint. It comprises four distinct muscular heads: rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, and vastus intermedius, all innervated by the posterior division of the femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4).
steps.say: The anterior thigh is dominated by the quadriceps femoris, the primary knee extensor. It consists of rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, and vastus intermedius, all innervated by the femoral nerve.

steps.tx: The rectus femoris is the only component of the quadriceps that crosses two joints. Arising by a straight head from the anterior inferior iliac spine and a reflected head from the ilium above the acetabulum, it functions as both a **hip flexor** and a powerful knee extensor, playing an active role during kicking and running.
steps.say: Rectus femoris is the sole quadriceps component crossing two joints. Arising from the anterior inferior iliac spine and acetabular margin, it flexes the hip and extends the knee during running and kicking.

steps.tx: Distal oblique fibers of vastus medialis insert directly into the medial border of the patella, designated the **vastus medialis obliquus** (VMO). These transverse fibers actively stabilize the patella during terminal knee extension, neutralizing the lateral dislocating vector generated by the quadriceps angle (Q-angle) to prevent recurrent patellar subluxation.
steps.say: The oblique fibers of vastus medialis form the vastus medialis obliquus, attaching to the medial patella. They counteract lateral pull from the quadriceps angle, preventing recurrent lateral patellar dislocation.

steps.tx: The **saphenous nerve** is the longest and largest cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve, carrying sensory fibres from L3 and L4. Descending through the adductor canal alongside the femoral vessels, it crosses the femoral artery from lateral to medial before piercing the subsartorial roof between sartorius and gracilis.
steps.say: The saphenous nerve is the longest cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve, derived from L3 and L4. It travels down the adductor canal with femoral vessels before piercing the fascia between sartorius and gracilis.

steps.tx: At the medial side of the knee, the saphenous nerve gives off the infrapatellar branch to supply skin over the tibial tuberosity, then accompanies the **great saphenous vein** down the medial leg. Stripping or harvesting the great saphenous vein for coronary bypass risks saphenous nerve injury, causing numbness over the medial leg and foot.
steps.say: At the knee, the saphenous nerve yields the infrapatellar branch before traveling with the great saphenous vein. Surgical harvesting or stripping of this vein can injure the nerve, creating numbness along the medial leg.

steps.tx: The medial compartment of the thigh comprises the adductor group: adductor longus, adductor brevis, adductor magnus, gracilis, and pectineus. These muscles are primarily innervated by the **obturator nerve** (L2, L3, L4), which arises from the anterior divisions of the lumbar plexus and enters the thigh through the obturator canal.
steps.say: The medial thigh adductor muscles are innervated by the obturator nerve, derived from lumbar roots L2 through L4. The nerve enters the thigh through the obturator canal to supply adductor longus, brevis, magnus, and gracilis.

rows: Adducts thigh, flexes and medially rotates leg

steps.tx: Upon exiting the obturator canal, the obturator nerve divides into anterior and posterior branches separated by the plane of **adductor brevis**. The anterior branch passes anterior to adductor brevis to supply gracilis and adductor longus, while the posterior branch pierces obturator externus and descends posterior to adductor brevis.
steps.say: Exiting the obturator canal, the obturator nerve splits around the adductor brevis into anterior and posterior branches. The anterior branch lies in front of adductor brevis, while the posterior branch runs behind it.

steps.tx: In addition to adductor motor control, the obturator nerve provides articular branches to both the hip and knee joints in accordance with Hilton law. Inflammation of the hip joint in pediatric patients (such as Perthes disease or septic arthritis) frequently presents as isolated **referred knee pain**, misleading unwary clinicians away from the diseased hip.
steps.say: The obturator nerve supplies sensory branches to both hip and knee joints. Under Hilton law, hip pathology in children often manifests exclusively as referred pain in the knee, obscuring primary hip pathology.
